events.description: U.S.-Taliban withdrawal agreement signed. The hosts say 'about three weeks' before recording; the date is resolved from the publish date. The hosts call it a withdrawal deal, not a peace deal.
Two Taliban spokesmen said on the day of signing that attacks on the Afghan government would continue.
Esper suggested Taliban 'hardliners' were failing to honor the reduction in violence, days after the Taliban stepped up attacks.
McKenzie told the Senate Armed Services Committee that a Taliban 'splinter' might be carrying out attacks ('last week').
Bill's tracking tally reached 248 Taliban-claimed attacks on Afghan forces in 28 of 34 provinces since the deal.
Taliban announced an offensive against ISIS in Kunar; Khalilzad praised it on Twitter and Suhail Shaheen rebutted him.
al-Qaeda released a three-page Arabic statement praising the Taliban's victory, calling Hibatullah 'emir of the faithful' and urging mujahideen to abide by the deal.
JNIM said it would negotiate with the Malian government if France leaves the region, citing the Taliban deal as a model.
AQIM's emir issued a video saying it would talk to regional governments as long as France withdraws.

key_claims: The U.S.-Taliban agreement is a withdrawal deal, not a peace deal. It has no ceasefire or reduction-in-violence provision.
U.S. officials (Esper, McKenzie) are 'wishcasting' by blaming rogue or splinter Taliban factions, although the Taliban publicly claims its attacks.
Taliban claims through 15 March 2020 covered 248 attacks in 28 of 34 provinces, probably only a quarter to half of the real total; there were zero Taliban attacks on al-Qaeda.
The Taliban fights ISIS because ISIS rejects its emirate; it has never denounced or attacked al-Qaeda, which has been loyal to the Emirate since the 1990s.
al-Qaeda celebrated the deal as a victory, called Hibatullah Akhundzada 'emir of the faithful', and told mujahideen to abide by it.
Al-Qaeda affiliates such as JNIM in Mali and AQIM are using the deal as a template to demand French withdrawal and negotiate with governments.
Mansour, the second Taliban emir, was close to al-Qaeda, and Hibatullah has not disavowed al-Qaeda's allegiance.
